paragraphs.text: A sermon by John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople. On the fig tree, for Great Monday. When the eye sees a flowering oak or a spring flowing strongly, it is drawn there by that sight, and the mind within the heart turns there too. Likewise, when the ear hears deeds and stories recounted in words, a person directs his thoughts toward them, so that his body is in one place, but his thoughts are in another, where the account depicts the event through its narrative. This is what has happened to me now, beloved. For as I hear the evangelist recount the deeds done by Christ in Bethany concerning the fig tree, I am here in body, but in my mind I place myself there. And I imagine myself now following in the footsteps of the Lord Jesus and seeing the fig tree, flourishing and bright before the Lord’s rebuke, but after the Lord’s rebuke, withered and dry. For it says, “In the morning, as Jesus was going into the city, he became hungry. And seeing a fig tree, he went to it and found nothing on it except leaves alone. And he said to it, ‘May no fruit ever come from you again.’ And immediately it withered there.” This has now been read to you. The event astonishes me; my mind is divided. For when

I wish to explain the events in the narrative, I am immediately drawn toward them by the sight of the miracle. It is like someone seeing a golden vessel containing a precious stone, with mysteries inscribed upon it: he wants to look at the vessel because of its brilliance, but is held back again by the stone within. For he is eager both to see the beauty of the stone and to understand the mystery inscribed upon it. So I too, seeing that the account of the event is radiant and beautiful, keep my mind there. Yet I am drawn back again by the spiritual vision, not to understand the miracles. For it says, “In the morning, as Jesus was passing into the city, he became hungry.” Oh, the unspeakable and unknowable mystery! He who feeds the whole world became hungry. He who fed five thousand to their fill with five loaves—he himself became hungry. He who by a single act of will changed water into wine for you became hungry. He who made living eyes from mud became hungry. He who walked upon the foam of the waves without wetting his foot in the water became hungry. He who brings souls out of bodies and brings them back again with a word. How then does Isaiah say, The eternal God neither hungers nor grows weary. But Christ is God in every respect [?]. to the one who believes and says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was

the Word.” How, then, did God hunger? He hungered in the form of a servant, yet he fed five thousand, in accordance with the sovereign will within him. He came to the fig tree as a visible man, yet he was everywhere in the divinity understood to be in him. As a man, he saw that the fig tree was fruitless; as God, he withered it with a word. He said, “Let there be no fruit from you ever again.” And the deed followed: immediately the fig tree began to wither there. The word was human, but the deed was divine. Yet it is very necessary, beloved, to investigate the image of the fig tree. Many have interpreted it, as it seems to me, but not according to the truth. Nevertheless, we will tell you the interpretations of those who came before us, and first present what we ourselves have labored over. For it is difficult to understand the meaning that lies in the written account, holding hidden in great depth [?] the radiance of a mystery. For what need was there for the fig tree to wither at a word, rather than bear fruit at a word? For he who withered it with a word could also have made it fruitful with a word. Or what sin did the fig tree commit, someone might ask, when it was not its season, since Mark the Evangelist says that it was winter at that time? And unless something mysterious was being done with it for humanity’s sake, the Lord himself will be found,

in one respect, praiseworthy because he withered it with a word, but blameworthy because he cursed it without reason. Yet it is right, beloved, to understand in this matter whose image he presented through the fig tree. For there was no deed done by Christ that did not contain a mystery enacted for humanity’s sake. For nothing was done by him in vain, no deed that was not beneficial, none that did not proclaim the truth, not one that did not move the mind toward heavenly understanding. Many interpreters have said that this fig tree represents the congregation of the Jews, to which, it says, the Lord came, seeking upon it the fruit of faith, and did not find it upon it, but only the words of the prophets and the Law. as though adorning itself with leaves. For this reason he withered it, saying, “May no fruit ever come from you again.” But I seek to argue against this interpretation, beloved. For this is not the true meaning. How could the Lord pronounce a curse, when he says, “Bless, and do not curse”? And how could he curse the synagogue and wither it, when he says, “The Son of Man did not come to destroy, but to seek and save what was lost”? But if anyone still objects and argues, saying that the fig tree is to be applied to the Jewish synagogue,

tell me how the synagogue, withered from its roots, brought forth the sweet Paul. There were also Aquila and Priscilla, and many others. I now pass over the names of the others in turn, to avoid making this discourse too long. And Paul bears witness for me that the Lord did not utterly reject the Jewish people, saying, “I ask, then, [?] has the Lord rejected his people? By no means! For I too am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. The Lord has not rejected his people.” Indeed, he also promised salvation to that people in the last days, as he says: “When the full number of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel will be saved.” For even if the Jews became enemies of God, they became so for our sake, so that we might receive mercy through their disobedience, as Paul bears witness for me, saying: “As regards the gospel,” he says, “they are enemies for your sake, but as regards election, they are beloved for the sake of the fathers. The gifts are irrevocable, and holy deliverance [?].” It is therefore fitting, beloved, to examine the saying about the fig tree, to see whose image it represented. But if you recall Adam, when he was stripped bare in Paradise, and which tree’s leaves he took and sewed together to make himself clothing, you will see how

he justly withered it. Was it not fig leaves that Adam took to cover his shame? So the Lord came, and the fig tree that had already entered into you, that covering of shame, he withered with a word. He took away your poverty and will give you riches. He took away the coverings of your shame and will give you clothing like snow, woven with water and the Spirit. He withered the fig tree’s leaves and will restore to you what your soul was deprived of. What was it deprived of? What the serpent took away in Paradise: a life equal to the angels’, the food of Paradise, the garment of incorruptibility. But let us return to the beginning. “In the morning,” it says, “as Jesus was going up to the city, he became hungry.” In the morning. When the night of deception passed, at dawn the light of Christ’s resurrection shone upon the world. For Christ is the dawn, as the prophet said: “We shall find him ready like the dawn.” In the morning, Jesus was going up into the city. In the morning, when dark death perished in the light of Christ’s glory, and the golden rays of the sun of righteousness shone in darkened hearts. In the morning, when he spread out the warm rays of his divinity and thawed the souls that the devil had put to death. There is nothing that can hide from his warmth. For the devil put human hearts to death through the cold of sin. Therefore the prophet prayed, saying:

“Set my innermost parts and my heart on fire.” For all humanity was bound by the cold of ungodliness. Therefore all the prophets prayed together to God, saying: “Restore us from captivity like streams in the south.” That is to say, just as the south wind, blowing warmly upon frozen waters, restores them to their original liquid state, so also with us, who have been put to death through the devil’s sin. And Christ’s grace, blowing like the south wind, restored us to our original state of incorruptibility. That warm blowing of the south wind the bride, the Church, also invokes in the Song of Songs, calling out and saying: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind. Blow through my garden, so that its sweet fragrances may flow.” “In the morning,” he said, “as Jesus was going up.” It is fitting that he says “going up,” to indicate [?] the prophet [?] Adam, who had fallen. Our Lord came again and was ascending to that same place. In the morning, as he was going up into the city. Now, when you hear “city,” do not look down below, but toward the Jerusalem above, the heavenly dwelling place. For [?] our life is in heaven. In the morning, as Jesus was going up into the city, he became hungry. He hungered not for human food, but for human life. “For my food,” he said, “is to do the will of my Father, so that they may believe in the one whom he sent.” For whoever believes in him, as he himself said, will never die.

In the morning, as Jesus was going up into the city, he became hungry, and seeing a fig tree, he approached it. It is good that he approached it. For if he had passed by the fig tree, the serpent would have had its nest in the fig tree without dying. But he approached the fig tree and withered it. The Lord [?] saw Nathanael beneath such a fig tree. For he said, “Before Philip called you, I saw you beneath the fig tree.” Long beforehand, the prophet spoke of this fig tree, which was to become fruitless: “I will go up among the people of my sojourn, because the fig tree bore no fruit.” Zacchaeus climbed such a fig tree to see the Lord. And he said to him, “Come down quickly.” The evangelist rightly spoke of a wild fig tree in connection with Zacchaeus, to indicate that the road is wide and spacious. It is wild and tangled, and from it comes an evil death. The Lord came to the fig tree. This fig tree was a symbol representing the wide and spacious road that leads to destruction. The fig leaf is flat and sharp. Sin is an irritation, leading to destruction across a wide and spacious sea. The fruit of the fig tree is sweet and slippery. Sweet is the pleasure that leads into sin. It tears apart those who approach it. Flee its taste. It is sweet to you when you taste it, but bitter after tasting. For honey drips

from the lips of a prostitute, who soothes your throat for a time. But afterward you will find it more bitter than gall and sharper than a double-edged sword. Pleasure is a prostitute. At first she speaks sweetly to you, secretly introducing deadly bitterness through her speech. Such was the serpent too: sweet in speech, but bitter in deceit. Sweet was the tasting, but bitter the fall. Flee pleasure, the prostitute, who speaks sweetly with you but fills you with bitter sores. Flee pleasure as Elijah fled Jezebel. The Lord came from heaven, thirsting for human life. He found the wide and spacious road that governs this life. He came to it. He found it adorned with leaves, but bearing no fruit of death. Why? Because it was not the season. For the evangelist added this: “For it had,” he said, “no fruit.” For it was not the season. How could it still produce deadly fruit when Jesus had come and was proclaiming resurrection to the world? It was not the season for it to produce deadly fruit. For death reigned from Adam to Moses, that is, until the Law. For Scripture is accustomed to call Moses the Law, as it says in the Gospel: “They have Moses and the prophets.” And what did the Lord say to it? “May there never be from you

any fruit forever.” And the fig tree withered, and Scripture was fulfilled. Death fell, defeated. Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O Hades, is your victory? Why, then, does the evangelist say that it was winter at that time, when the fig tree was adorned with leaves? But [?], offering protection, while sin was still flourishing, the devil’s snow lay over all humanity. For before the ruler of the world, Christ, came, the human race, suffering many ailments, [?] into worship at pagan temples, into songs, and into lusting after women. But when the Lord, our peace, came, he swept away the impurities of hostile people, which churn up the salty sea of this life’s pleasures, and the foaming waves of the passions. He withered the fig tree and planted the cross, blossoming with faith and shining with life for everyone. The roots of this cross were set in the earth, while [?] were raised to heaven. Its foliage does not age, its blossom does not wither, and its fruit is deathless. David also mentions this tree, saying: “And he will be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which will yield its fruit in its season, and its leaf will not fall.” Wisdom also mentions this tree, saying: “She is a tree of life to all who hold fast to her.” This tree

Jeremiah saw with a prophet’s eye as something the Jews intended to prepare for Christ; he spoke directly to the Jews, saying to them: “Come, let us put wood into his bread, and let us wipe him out from the land of the living.” The wood is the cross; the bread is Christ’s flesh. The Lord took bread and said: “This is my flesh, broken for you for the forgiveness of sins.” Stretching out his hands on this tree of the cross and scattering the powers that hover in the air, he prepared an unobstructed journey to heaven for us, setting up faith as a ladder for us from earth to heaven. And this is wonderful, if you listen, beloved: the tree of the cross stood, and on it was crucified the true vine, who says: “I am the vine.” It became a vine of death for the devil, but a vine of life for us. It became for us a God-bearing vine, sheltering us from the burning heat of our sins and giving us rest like shade. The one sitting in its shade repeats the words spoken by Solomon: “I desired his shade and sat down, and its fruit is sweet to my [?].” Trusting in this shade, blessed David said: “In the shadow of your wings I will place my hope.” For how long? “Until my lawlessness passes away.” O wondrous deed and new mystery! There was a spring on the tree, and from it the cross

was watered. For when he was pierced in the side with a spear, he poured out blood and water. And with water he watered its roots, so that it might forever bloom with immortal fruits for those who believe. O blessed tree, which kings honor and rulers and nobles love, as do men and women, and all nature and humankind. It has a guardian whom demons dread and before whom the devil trembles. The angels praise him, and the heavens bless him; the apostles proclaim him, and the churches sing of the Lord Christ, who was crucified upon it. To him be glory and dominion, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
